documents: Published paper PDF, Ore Geology Reviews 147 (2022) 104972, 17 pages
Publisher XML converted to located text (jats_text); contains only the abstract header, figure captions (Fig. 1 to Fig. 12) and table captions (Table 1, Table 2), no body paragraphs
pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (they coincide with the printed journal pages 1 to 17) for body text, because the supplied XML text holds no body paragraphs. Figure captions are cited by the caption label exactly as printed in the XML text (e.g. 'Fig. 7'), with the PDF page in parentheses.

entry.evidence: we examined the relationship between the fault-fracture networks and auriferous vein systems to better understand the role of brittle structures

sequences.source_document: Published paper PDF with XML caption text

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how the fault-fracture network controlled mineralizing fluid flow in a well-exposed Au-Ag vein system. They take as a premise that oblique sinistral-normal faults control the mineralization.
steps.quote: Our main objective was to gain a better understanding of the mechanisms of mineralizing fluid flow

steps.action: The authors take the geological setting, grades, K-Ar ages and fluid-inclusion and isotope constraints of the deposit from earlier studies.
steps.quote: Fluid inclusion and stable isotope (oxygen and hydrogen) studies by Kim et al. (2002)

steps.action: The authors design the survey: 1:5,000 mapping, grid mapping of six vein-filled fault systems, and traverse lines normal to the fault trend. Veins are classified as mode-I or hybrid, and the design adds box-counting (BENOIT) and linear-traverse fractal analyses.
steps.quote: we performed a traverse-line survey (set normal to the main trend of faults or veins) to understand the fault zone architectures of each VF

steps.action: The authors map vertical and horizontal outcrops of six example vein-filled faults, recording vein thickness, geometry and marker-bed offsets. They also assay 16 samples for Au and Ag.
steps.quote: Geochemical analyses for the LNV yielded maximum Au and Ag values of 8.69 and 99.39 ppm, respectively.

steps.action: The authors infer normal slip on the vein-filled faults from subvertical mode-I veins in the damage zones, using Andersonian stress reasoning.
steps.quote: the presence of subvertical veins in the damage zones (Fig. 4c, e) indicate a normal sense movement along the VF

steps.action: The authors check the slip sense inferred from vein geometry against the independent offset of key marker beds.
steps.quote: [...] based on the vein geometry is also consistent with the slip sense of key beds.

steps.action: From mode-I veins in linking damage zones and from thickness changes at fault bends on horizontal outcrops, the authors infer sinistral motion. They conclude that the system is an oblique normal-sinistral fault system.
steps.quote: the VF in the LNV area was interpreted as an oblique slip (normal-sinistral) fault system

steps.action: Along the 80 m LNV traverse the authors record vein number, vein thickness, dip separation and fracture number. They plot cumulative frequencies and delimit six fault-related damage zones.
steps.quote: Based on the changes in cumulative frequency, this system could be divided into six fault-related damage zones

steps.action: The authors interpret Fault 10 as the main fault, with antithetic and synthetic subsidiary faults, forming a NE-trending full graben with sinistral shear.
steps.quote: the VF was interpreted as a NE-trending full-graben system with sinistral shear sense.

steps.action: The authors estimate box-counting fractal dimensions (with SD) for 18 boxes over different fault architectures. They quantify vein density per box in ArcGIS.
steps.quote: Eighteen box-counting analyses were performed in this study

steps.action: The authors compare D-values across vein types and against vein density. They find higher D for mixed fault-plane plus damage-zone veins and a roughly proportional D-density relation, with stated exceptions (B4 vs B2, B13 vs B12).
steps.quote: Vein density and D-values show a directly proportional relationship.

steps.action: The authors propose that the degree of space filling, and hence the D-value, is governed by damage-zone development and type.
steps.quote: the degree of space filling was interpreted to be affected by the development of the damage zone

steps.action: The authors fit power laws to the cumulative vein-thickness distribution of 92 LNV veins. They find slope breaks defining Domains I to III, with D = 0.497, 1.25 and 0.62.
steps.quote: the slope change indicating more than two D-values was confirmed to be in the ranges

steps.action: The authors ask what controls the slope change (scale transition) in the thickness distribution.
steps.quote: further analysis was undertaken to understand the slope change as follows.

steps.action: Plotting vein type by thickness domain, the authors propose that mixing of mode-I and hybrid veins causes the Domain I to II break. For Domain III they set this against a censoring-effect artifact and a vein-type control.
steps.quote: the low correlation coefficient of Domain III could be interpreted as an erroneous D-value by a censoring effect

steps.action: The authors analyse independent LV thickness data (from Kim, 2016) in the same way, separately for hanging wall and footwall, to validate the LNV scale property. The main 13 m vein is excluded.
steps.quote: To validate and compare the scale property of the LNV traverse

steps.action: The authors compare the LV with the LNV result and find similar slope breaks and a zigzag zone in the hanging-wall data, but not in the footwall data. LV veins could not be typed.
steps.quote: the LV graph shows a scale transition in the zigzag zone similar to that of the LNV graph

steps.action: Along three mapped fault architectures (Fig. 11) the authors compare cumulative vein thickness along regularly spaced lines. They find thicker totals across damage zones (ratio up to 3.15) and a distribution width that depends on damage-zone type.
steps.quote: the total thickness of the vein was found to be thicker across the damaged area

steps.action: The authors remove hybrid veins and refit the LNV thickness distribution of mode-I veins only. They find no noticeable slope change.
steps.quote: no noticeable slope change in the mode-I veins of the LNV could be distinguished

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that mixing of mode-I and hybrid veins controls the scale transition and that secondary fault damage zones control vein distribution and fluid flow.
steps.quote: we find that the mixing of mode-I and hybrid veins is an important controlling factor for scale transition

Conditions found in outcrop traces of a past hydrothermal-faulting event

Survives the LV comparison and the hybrid-removal test; the censoring rival is not resolved
Kept: damage zones control vein density; vein-type mixing causes the scale transition

end.claim: Vein density and physical properties are strongly controlled by the types, or existence, of fault damage zones, and the scale transition in vein thickness arises from hybrid veins filling secondary fault planes.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the detailed grid mapping and traverse classification of veins by type and damage zone there would be no basis for linking D-values and slope breaks to fault architecture.

gates.evidence: Action: the premise that oblique faults control mineralization directed traverses normal to the faults (p. 3, p. 5), but no rival hypothesis guided acquisition. Claim: the mode-I-only refit could have shown a slope break and the LV data could have differed (pp. 10-16); the censoring rival for Domain III was left open. Registration: nothing is stated as fixed before the data.

imports.item: Mode I, shear and hybrid fracture classification (Ramsay and Chester, 2004)

imports.field: software (used e.g. in palaeontology, Lehane and Ekdale 2013)

imports.item: INAA and ICP-MS assays at Actlabs

limits: The XML text supplied contains only captions, so body locations are PDF pages. Sub-claims at other statuses: the oblique normal-sinistral kinematics and full-graben geometry are best_explanation (pp. 6, 8). The D-value versus vein-density relation is regularity_in_range, holding 'in most cases' over 18 boxes with stated exceptions (p. 8). The box D-values are estimate_with_resolution, with SD given (Fig. 7). The censoring-effect rival for the Domain II to III break is raised but not excluded (p. 10). The LV comparison uses data from Kim (2016), a co-author's thesis, and the LV veins could not be typed, so the hybrid-mixing mechanism is untested there (pp. 12-13). Fault 10's displacement could not be measured (p. 8). The 1 mm thickness cutoff and the choice of slope-break locations are not tested. The acknowledgements mention anonymous reviewers and an associate editor, but no review file was supplied, so changes made in review cannot be coded. No statistical test of the fitted slopes is reported. Inference: the slope breaks appear to be placed by visual inspection.

disagreements.target: The general expectation that cumulative vein-thickness distributions follow a single power law (e.g. Sanderson et al., 1994; Roberts et al., [...]
disagreements.support: LNV and LV thickness data show multiple slopes, and removing hybrid veins restores a single slope for mode-I veins.
disagreements.quote: the presence of hybrid veins that fill secondary fault planes, which disturbs the original linear relationship shown by cumulative thickness distribution data

disagreements.target: The view from fracture-mechanics rules that veins form in extension fractures
disagreements.support: The authors cite Belayneh and Cosgrove (2010) and classify their own veins into mode-I and hybrid types with distinct geometries.
disagreements.quote: veins and dykes are typically considered as having formed in extension fractures. However, veins can also develop within hybrid fractures

alternatives_considered.chosen: Vein-type difference (Domain III all hybrid veins) as a potential control of the Domain II to III slope change
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Erroneous D-value from a censoring effect (low correlation coefficient)
alternatives_considered.reason: Domain III was comprised of only hybrid veins, unlike the other domains

alternatives_considered.chosen: Exclude the 13 m main Lighthouse vein from the LV thickness data
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Include it in the hanging-wall and footwall data
alternatives_considered.reason: to avoid duplicate calculations in the HW and FW
